_comment: An idea's history told as a book of episodes (campaign.md, and its §6 for a campaign that is not a war). Each season is one story folder, scouted, planned, written and finished like any episode; the book reads them in order. The seasons' `when`, `edge`, `pivotal`, `aliases` and `start` are LEADS, as in candidates.json: never facts and never a ranking. A scout establishes each from fetched sources and the edge re-check tries to refute it, priority and legend included. The working title and subtitle are the author's to change; the question is proposed by the scout's outline.
title: A Pivotal History of Mathematics
subtitle: Problems people needed solved, and the ideas that solved them, from the record
author: Lawrence, 2026-11-21: "I think for pivotal histories I would like to do a history of mathematics, can you please outline and begin on this". And: "if we run out of my weekly claude code subscription then you can stop, do not use API Key calls to continue".
_question: Proposed by the scout's outline as one short line in the author's voice (16 words at most), written here only when he has approved it (campaign.md §4).
_world: The seasons' shared world pool, stories/_world/history-of-mathematics/ (history/jobs/world.md): what a scribe's school was, a counting board, the Museum at Alexandria, a merchant's abacus school, a public problem contest. A fact one season tells, no other season tells again.

mainAccounts.note: LEAD: the mathematician's own text, in an old translation, is the season's main account and its `ownWords` (campaign.md §6): the reader is placed, by declaration, at the page or the table where the work was done. Every translation's date and licence is the scout's to establish: a work first published in the United States, or abroad, before 1931 is a lead for `pd`, never a verdict. Where only a later writer tells the story (Iamblichus on the Pythagoreans, Plutarch on Archimedes), that writer is attributed with their distance from the events.

seasons.subject: A Pivotal History of Mathematics, c. 1550 BC: the Rhind papyrus and the scribes' reckoning
seasons.edge: Technical: written methods a trained scribe could follow without understanding why they worked: multiplying by doubling, fractions as sums of unit fractions, a guessed answer corrected in proportion ('false position'), set out as worked problems about bread, beer, granaries and pyramids. Babylon's base-sixty place-value tablets, with a square root of two good to about six decimal places, as the world around it
seasons.pivotal: The oldest long mathematical text to survive; Greek writers said their geometry began in Egypt, where the Nile's floods made land be measured again each year (Herodotus, book II)
start: internet-archive: Peet, The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus, British Museum 10057 and 10058 (1923)
internet-archive: Chace, The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus (Mathematical Association of America, 1927–1929)
gutenberg: Herodotus, Histories, book II (Macaulay)
wikipedia: Rhind Mathematical Papyrus; YBC 7289; Plimpton 322 (leads and references only)

seasons.subject: A Pivotal History of Mathematics, c. 450–369 BC: the diagonal no number measures
seasons.edge: Scientific: proof. A square's side and its diagonal have no common measure, however small, and an argument from odd and even numbers shows it must be so; Theodorus and Theaetetus went on to the square roots of other numbers
seasons.pivotal: Greek mathematics turned from counting to geometry and to proof from stated starting points, the road to Euclid (Plato, Aristotle; Heath)
seasons.doubt: Pythagoras left no writing and the discovery's story (Hippasus drowned for telling it) is told by writers some eight hundred years later. The re-check weighs legend against record; the idea stays whoever found it.

internet-archive: Heath, A History of Greek Mathematics, volume 1 (1921)
internet-archive: Iamblichus, Life of Pythagoras (Thomas Taylor, 1818)
internet-archive: Aristotle, Prior Analytics (Oxford translation, 1928 or earlier)
wikipedia: Hippasus; Theaetetus (mathematician) (leads and references only)

seasons.subject: A Pivotal History of Mathematics, c. 300–240 BC: Alexandria, Euclid and Eratosthenes
seasons.edge: Scientific: a few definitions and postulates stated first, and everything else proved from them in order (the Elements); then geometry turned on the world, the Earth's size worked out from the angle of a noon shadow and the distance between two towns
seasons.pivotal: The Elements was the way geometry was taught for some two thousand years; Eratosthenes' measure showed a geometer could size the Earth from a city
start: internet-archive: Heath, The Thirteen Books of Euclid's Elements (1908)
internet-archive: Proclus, The Philosophical and Mathematical Commentaries on the First Book of Euclid's Elements (Thomas Taylor, 1792)
internet-archive: Heath, Aristarchus of Samos (1913), for Cleomedes' account of Eratosthenes
wikipedia: Euclid's Elements; Eratosthenes (leads and references only)

seasons.subject: A Pivotal History of Mathematics, c. 250–212 BC: Archimedes, the circle and the sand
seasons.edge: Scientific: the circle squeezed between polygons of ninety-six sides to pin its ratio between three and ten seventy-firsts and three and a seventh; a way of naming numbers big enough to count the sand that would fill the universe; shapes weighed against each other on an imagined balance to find their areas and volumes
seasons.pivotal: His methods came nearest the calculus of anything before it; The Method, lost for centuries, was read under a prayer book's text in 1906 (Heiberg). Cicero found his overgrown tomb at Syracuse in 75 BC by the sphere and cylinder carved on it
seasons.doubt: The Siege of Syracuse (syracuse-213bc) is already the series' telling of his engines and the city's fall: this season never retells it. A callback to it is a claim from this story's own sources (campaign.md §3). His last words to a soldier are told differently by Plutarch and others: a legend, attributed.
start: internet-archive: Heath, The Works of Archimedes (1897)
internet-archive: Heath, The Method of Archimedes, recently discovered by Heiberg (1912)
gutenberg: Plutarch, Life of Marcellus (Dryden, rev. Clough)
gutenberg: Cicero, Tusculan Disputations, book V (Yonge, 1877)

seasons.subject: A Pivotal History of Mathematics, AD 499–876: India, and zero becomes a number
seasons.edge: Scientific: nine digits and a zero, each worth what its place makes it; and in Brahmagupta's book of 628, rules for adding, subtracting and multiplying with zero and with negative numbers, called debts beside fortunes
seasons.pivotal: The decimal place-value numerals the world now writes; a temple inscription at Gwalior dated 876 writes a zero as a digit

internet-archive: Clark, The Aryabhatiya of Aryabhata (University of Chicago, 1930)
internet-archive: Smith and Karpinski, The Hindu-Arabic Numerals (1911)
wikipedia: Brahmagupta; Chaturbhuj Temple, Gwalior; Bakhshali manuscript (leads and references only)

seasons.subject: A Pivotal History of Mathematics, c. AD 820: Baghdad, al-Khwarizmi and al-jabr
seasons.edge: Scientific: problems of inheritance, trade and measuring land written as equations of a few standard kinds and solved by two moves, al-jabr (restoring) and al-muqabala (balancing), each rule justified by a square drawn and completed
seasons.pivotal: The word algebra comes from his book's title and algorithm from his name; his book on the Indian numerals carried them to Latin Europe
start: internet-archive: Rosen, The Algebra of Mohammed ben Musa (1831)
internet-archive: Karpinski, Robert of Chester's Latin Translation of the Algebra of al-Khowarizmi (1915)
internet-archive: Smith and Karpinski, The Hindu-Arabic Numerals (1911)
wikipedia: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi; House of Wisdom (leads and references only)

seasons.subject: A Pivotal History of Mathematics, 1202–1299: Pisa, and the numerals reach the merchants
seasons.edge: Technical: reckoning written on paper with the Indian numerals in place of the counting board and Roman numerals, taught through merchants' own problems: exchange, partnership, interest, and a pair of rabbits
seasons.pivotal: Italian abacus schools taught the numerals to merchants' sons; Florence's money-changers forbade them in account books in 1299
seasons.doubt: Liber Abaci has no English translation old enough to be clean; the season may rest on the Latin edition and later writers. The scout says whether it carries a season, a short one, or folds into the sixth.

seasons.subject: A Pivotal History of Mathematics, 1535–1548: the cubic duels
seasons.edge: Scientific: a rule for solving cubic equations, kept secret because it won public problem contests, handed over under an oath, then printed in Ars Magna (1545) with the quartic beside it
seasons.pivotal: The first solution Europe's mathematicians could claim past the ancients; the square roots of negative numbers it could not avoid began the complex numbers (Bombelli, 1572). Ferrari and Tartaglia met in a public disputation at Milan in 1548

seasons.subject: A Pivotal History of Mathematics, 1614–1627: Napier's logarithms
seasons.edge: Technical: tables that turn multiplication and division into addition and subtraction, computed by hand over years; Briggs's tables to base ten after his visit to Napier
seasons.pivotal: Kepler computed the Rudolphine Tables with them (1627); logarithm tables and the slide rule did the long sums of navigation, astronomy and engineering until electronic calculators

seasons.subject: A Pivotal History of Mathematics, 1654: Pascal, Fermat and the problem of points
seasons.edge: Scientific: an unfinished game's stakes split fairly by counting every way it could have ended; two methods by letter, Fermat's by listing the cases and Pascal's by working back from the end
seasons.pivotal: A mathematics of chance: Huygens's book on games of chance followed in 1657, and probability went on to insurance and statistics

seasons.subject: A Pivotal History of Mathematics, 1665–1716: the calculus and the war over it
seasons.edge: Scientific: methods for how fast a quantity changes and for the area under a curve, found by Newton and by Leibniz each on his own, and Leibniz's notation that let others use them
seasons.pivotal: Physics and engineering came to run on the calculus; the Royal Society's report of 1712 found for Newton, who had written it, and the quarrel parted British mathematics from the Continent's

seasons.subject: A Pivotal History of Mathematics, 1801–1802: finding Ceres
seasons.edge: Scientific: an orbit worked out from a few weeks of sightings of a new planet that had been lost in the Sun's glare, by a young Gauss, with what he later published as the method of least squares
seasons.pivotal: Ceres was found again close to where Gauss had said, at the turn of 1802; least squares became the way every science fits a line to measurements

wikipedia: Ceres (dwarf planet), discovery; Least squares, history (leads and references only)

seasons.subject: A Pivotal History of Mathematics, 1823–1832: a strange new universe
seasons.edge: Scientific: Euclid's parallel postulate dropped, and a geometry built without it that held together, by Bolyai in Hungary and Lobachevsky in Kazan, each on his own; Gauss wrote that he had thought the same and not published
seasons.pivotal: Geometry stopped being one truth about space; Riemann's lecture of 1854 opened the curved geometry that general relativity uses

seasons.subject: A Pivotal History of Mathematics, 1913–1920: a letter from Madras
seasons.edge: Scientific: formulas found with little formal training, sent from a clerk's desk in Madras to Cambridge in a letter, and proved, sharpened or corrected with Hardy
seasons.pivotal: Ramanujan was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1918; his notebooks were still being worked through after he died in 1920

seasons.subject: A Pivotal History of Mathematics, 1900–1936: the limits of proof
seasons.edge: Scientific: Hilbert's programme to put all of mathematics on proven foundations, and the proofs that it cannot be done: Gödel's (1931), that a consistent system rich enough for arithmetic holds truths it cannot prove, and Turing's (1936), that no machine can decide every statement, with the universal machine the proof needed
seasons.pivotal: Turing's universal machine is the model of the stored-program computer, and his war work at Bletchley Park followed
seasons.doubt: Gödel's and Turing's papers are under copyright in English (Turing's may be public in the UK since 2025: the scout establishes it). The season may be facts-only for its climax, so L0 there.

bench._comment: Episodes left out of the first outline, for the author to swap in (campaign.md §6). Leads, like the seasons.
leads: Kerala, c. 1350–1530: Madhava's infinite series for pi and the sine, centuries before Europe (Whish, Transactions of the Royal Asiatic Society, 1834); weak on what changed after
China, AD 263 and the 5th century: Liu Hui and Zu Chongzhi bound pi (no old English translation; facts-only)
Isfahan, c. 1070: Omar Khayyam solves cubics with conic sections (Kasir's translation, 1931: public in the US from 2027)
Königsberg, 1736: Euler and the seven bridges (Latin original; English translations under copyright)
Paris, 1832: Galois's letter the night before his duel (French; the legend outgrew the record)
London, 1843: Ada Lovelace's notes on Babbage's engine (Scientific Memoirs, 1843; Babbage, Passages from the Life of a Philosopher, 1864); the engine was never built
Göttingen, 1915–1918: Emmy Noether's theorem on symmetry and conservation (German original, 1918, public)
Warsaw and Bletchley, 1932–1941: the mathematicians who broke Enigma (NSA Center for Cryptologic History, public); a codebreak the war books could tell
1637–1995: Fermat's note in his Diophantus (Heath, Diophantus of Alexandria, 1910) and Wiles's proof (facts only)
